title: Metaphor: seeing the light
subtitle: the urban jungle, on the ball, cast light on
summary: See how English uses words in abstract rather than literal ways - light for understanding, temperature for feeling, water for crowds - and use the everyday metaphors built on them.

lesson.heading: What metaphors are
lesson.text: **Metaphor** is using words in abstract rather than literal ways. It expresses something by comparing it indirectly with something else that has similar characteristics. Call a city a **jungle** and you suggest that, literally like a jungle, it is wild and full of dangers. Say that someone **lights up your life** and you suggest that, literally like a light, they make your life brighter and happier.

examples.text: When the writer refers to the urban **jungle**, he suggests that the city is dangerous and unpleasant.

lesson.heading: Idioms built on metaphors
lesson.text: Many idioms are metaphorical expressions in common use. To **be on the ball** is to be very aware of things and ready to act - literally, like a footballer who is always where the ball is. To **keep someone on a tight rein** is to have a lot of control over them - literally, like a rider holding a horse's reins tightly.

examples.text: Joe is always **on the ball**; he always knows what's going on.
I'm afraid we need to keep a **tight rein** on our spending this year.
Oscar's going to be **holding the reins** while the boss is on holiday.
examples.note: holding the reins = in charge; from horse riding

lesson.heading: Metaphors from parts of the body
rows: the organ at the body's centre
the place where a river joins the sea
be good at finding a bargain
a calculation that is not exact but accurate enough
lesson.note: Rights go hand in hand with responsibilities.

lesson.heading: Five metaphorical concepts English lives by
rows: a **bright** person, a **dim** person, **see the light**, **cast light on** a subject
**blow hot and cold**, a **hotheaded** reaction, a **cold-hearted** man, **keep cool**
people **flooding** out of a hall, a few **trickling** in, a constant **stream** of traffic
**spend** an hour, **waste** time, **save** half an hour, **invest** time that will **pay dividends**
a marketing **strategy**, clever **tactics**, **launch** an advertising **campaign**, sales **targets**
lesson.note: These are so common that English speakers no longer notice they are metaphors.

lesson.heading: Light and temperature in use
lesson.text: Because understanding is pictured as light, a clever person is **bright** and a less intelligent one **dim**. If you **see the light**, you finally understand. To **cast** or **throw light on** something is to make it easier to understand. Because feeling is pictured as heat, a **hotheaded** person reacts on feeling without thinking, and a **cold-hearted** one seems to have no feelings at all.

examples.text: The discovery of the poet's letters has **cast light on** his troubled relationship with his brother.
This book **throws a great deal of fresh light on** the history of the period.
I never used to understand opera, but an excellent TV series helped me to **see the light**.
Try to **keep cool** even if he argues with you.

lesson.heading: More metaphorical idioms and where their image comes from
rows: change the rules while something is going on
an idea that is not fully thought through
likely to complete a planned course of action
the moving hands of a clock
accept them as they appear, without suspecting more
a coin or stamp, whose value is printed on its face

lesson.heading: Metaphor in literature
lesson.text: More unusual and original metaphors are used a great deal in literature. Shakespeare's are among the best known in English, and each works by holding a literal picture against an abstract idea.

examples.text: *All the world's a **stage** and all the men and women merely **players**.*
examples.note: life is like a theatre; people have roles to play that may be written in advance

examples.text: *We are such **stuff** as dreams are made on, and our little life is rounded with a **sleep**.*
examples.note: our lives have as little substance as a dream, and death is likened to sleep

examples.text: *There is a **tide** in the affairs of men, which, taken at the **flood**, leads on to fortune.*
examples.note: our lives have tides like the sea, and we must catch the lucky opportunity at its height

lesson.text: When an idiom puzzles you, picture it literally first - a rider's reins, a hot head, a ship being loaded - and the figurative meaning usually follows.

exercises.prompt: Helen asked me to keep a close ___ on her little boy while the children were playing in the garden.
exercises.explanation: To keep a close eye on someone is to watch them carefully.

exercises.prompt: You don't need to worry about your grandfather - he's in safe ___ in the hospital.
exercises.explanation: In safe hands means the person in charge is capable.

exercises.prompt: Our hotel offers excellent facilities in the ___ of the old city centre.
exercises.explanation: The heart of a city is its centre.

exercises.prompt: When the writer refers to the urban ___, he is suggesting that the city is a dangerous and unpleasant place.
exercises.hint: (a wild place full of trees and animals)
exercises.explanation: Calling a city a jungle suggests it is wild and full of dangers.

exercises.prompt: As a rule of ___, you can expect to deal with about 20 orders a day.
exercises.explanation: A rule of thumb is a calculation that is not exact but accurate enough.

exercises.prompt: Joe is always on the ___; he always knows what's going on.
exercises.hint: (what a footballer keeps his eye on)
exercises.explanation: To be on the ball is to be very aware and ready to act.

exercises.prompt: Can you see that small boat at the ___ of the river?
exercises.explanation: The mouth of a river is where it joins the sea.

exercises.prompt: It is up to the ___ of the school how the budget is spent.
exercises.explanation: The head of an organisation is the person in charge.

exercises.prompt: I never used to understand opera, but an excellent TV series helped me to see the ___.
exercises.explanation: To see the light is to understand something at last.

exercises.prompt: Each idiom draws its image from an area of life. Match them.
Which metaphorical concept does each sentence draw on?

items.text: This book throws fresh light on the history of the period.
Her explanation cast light on the problem.
We could save half an hour if we went through the wood.
Don't waste time arguing with him.
We spent months on the project.
Police tried to control the flow of the fans as they left the concert.
There was a constant stream of traffic past the window.
People were flooding out of the hall.

exercises.prompt: Try to keep cool even if he argues with you. Which concept is this metaphor based on?
exercises.explanation: Keep cool means keep calm - strong feeling is pictured as heat.

exercises.prompt: We spent months trying to achieve our sales targets. Which two concepts appear here?
options: time is money, and business is a military operation
understanding is light, and time is money
business is war, and people are water
feeling is temperature, and time is money
exercises.explanation: You spend time as you spend money, and targets belong to the language of military operations.

exercises.statement: If someone blows hot and cold, they are enthusiastic at one time and not at another.
exercises.explanation: Correct - intensity of feeling is pictured as temperature.

exercises.statement: A hotheaded person is one who thinks carefully before reacting.
exercises.explanation: A hotheaded person reacts quickly on the basis of their feelings without thinking first.

exercises.prompt: Put this famous Shakespeare metaphor in order.
exercises.answer: All the world's a stage and all the men and women merely players
exercises.explanation: Life is compared to a theatre in which everyone has a part to play.
